title: Pastels au Poisson
author: Au Sénégal (le cœur du Sénégal) — column ‘Les douceurs d’Ève’
desc: Half-moon turnovers of a plain flour dough filled with sardinella or tuna cooked down with onion, garlic and tomato paste, deep-fried and served with a hot onion-tomato sauce.
longDesc: The page that fixes the vocabulary: in Senegal the traditional pastel is a small fried turnover filled with fish, most often sardinella or tuna, and nearly always served with a lightly spiced tomato sauce of onions and chilli that is ‘an integral part of the tasting’. A fataya, by the same page, is generally the same turnover filled with minced beef — though in practice names vary by family and neighbourhood, and some people use the two words interchangeably. The dough here is the plainest of the four printed in this collection: flour, water, a little sugar and milk powder, salt, no egg and no fat. Fish and onions are softened in oil with garlic and tomato paste, the dough is rolled out, filled, folded to half-moons, sealed with a fork and fried; the sauce is onions cooked down with tomato paste and chilli.
ingredients: 1 large tin sardinella (or tuna), about 400 g
Salt, pepper and seasoning cube — quantities not printed
Oil for softening the onions — quantity not printed
Salt, pepper and seasoning cube — quantities not printed
Oil for deep-frying — quantity not printed
steps: Soften the onions in oil. Add the flaked sardinella (or tuna), the garlic and the tomato paste with a little water, and simmer. Season with salt, pepper, chilli and the seasoning cube. Let it cool.
Mix the flour, milk powder, sugar and salt. Add the water gradually until the dough is soft and firm but not sticky. Rest it briefly (no time printed).
Flatten small portions into circles. Put a spoonful of filling on each, fold into half-moons and seal the edges with a fork.
Deep-fry over medium heat until golden on both sides. Drain.
Cook the onions with the tomato paste and chilli, add a little water, and simmer until smooth. Season.
Serve the pastels hot with the sauce and, if you like, a fresh salad.
chefTips: The dough target is ‘soft, firm, not sticky’ — add the water gradually rather than all at once.
The page prints neither a frying temperature nor a frying time. Judge by the colour: golden on both sides.
Seal the edges firmly with a fork so the filling does not escape in the oil.
commonMistakes: Adding all the water at once and ending with a sticky dough.
Frying over very high heat, which colours the dough before it is cooked.
Under-seasoning the filling — the sauce is meant to be spicy but the filling carries the fish.
storage: Best eaten the day they are fried; keeps 1 day in the fridge.
reheating: Recrisp in a hot oven for 8 to 10 minutes.
healthBenefits: Sardinella and tuna supply protein and omega-3 fats.
Tomato paste adds lycopene to the filling and the sauce.
culturalNote: The page’s own distinction — pastel for fish, fataya for minced meat — is the one most Senegalese cooks would recognise, but the source says outright that usage varies by family and neighbourhood. Fataya is of Lebanese origin; the Mbaye pages in this research say it has become so embedded in Senegalese cooking that its origin is forgotten.
